prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep B030 as my single-part position and I now hold it on the science and on the credit, not only because the opening count favoured it. The achievement is a precision instrument built on one clean idea: at the magic wavelength the lattice light shift cancels, so thousands of atoms can be interrogated at once without Doppler or recoil broadening. The hard part, which I respect as an instrument builder, was the control of blackbody, collisional and lattice-light systematics down to about 10^-18. That level has been reproduced and surpassed in several independent laboratories (Tokyo, Boulder, Paris, Braunschweig and others), and cross-laboratory comparisons agree. Those comparisons are the independent confirmation I look for in any claimed result. The credit is the cleanest on the shortlist: Katori proposed the scheme and made the first demonstration, and Ye took it to record accuracy and the many-body regime. All seven members who proposed laureates named exactly these two, and no other candidate comes close to that. I would word the citation around the magic-wavelength lattice clock itself, so that it cannot be read as a third comb or ion-clock prize, and I would keep prospective uses such as the redefinition of the second out of the citation.
statement.case_against: The reservation that I take most seriously, and that Olsson, Kroll, Lindroth, Johansson and Eriksson each raise in some form, is that this is a precision-measurement invention built beside the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and it may read as incremental or as technology rather than discovery of a new phenomenon. I answer that the lattice clock is a distinct scheme with distinct physics, but I accept this is a judgment on which reasonable members differ and not a point I can prove. The priority of Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley and others is not closed by anything in the record I have, and the share between Katori and Ye will have to be described carefully. The societal payoff is still prospective until the second is redefined. Finally, I am not an atomic physicist, so my own comparison with the earlier prizes carries less weight than that of Lindroth and Kroll.

responses.point: Olsson now supports B030 but asks whether a record in precision is a discovery at all, and whether the clock is separate enough from Hall and Hansch's comb and Wineland's ion work. She also keeps B020 as a strong alternative if reviewers can document who did the original work.
responses.response: I think the statutory test is met, because the Statute speaks of discovery or invention, and the magic-wavelength lattice is an invention that changed what can be measured. The comb is a tool the clock uses, and Wineland's work concerns single trapped ions, so neither is the same scheme. I agree with her that we must not lean on prospective uses. I would drop them from the citation. On B020, I thank her for her openness. I cannot yet give her the documentation she asks for, because AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND leave the three-name question open. A request to expert reviewers is the right way to settle it, and I would put it to them for any future round.

responses.point: Kroll ranks B030 first, but in his reply to me keeps IceCube last, because source identification still rests on two or three objects at moderate significance and credit within a collaboration of hundreds is unresolved. He also discloses a mentor-lineage link to Ye's field.
responses.response: I accept his second point in full. The credit problem for IceCube is real, and that is why I no longer press it ahead of B030. On the first point I still hold that the diffuse flux is a discovery in its own right and is confirmed in several channels, but I concede that the astronomy that follows is not settled. On his disclosure, a year in Hall's laboratory long ago is a distant link and no collaboration. I do not think it requires recusal, though the committee should record it, and I would prefer his judgement to Ye's priority to be heard.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from B058 to B030 but says that if the committee values a new state of matter over an instrument he would not object to B058, and that the credited names omit Lemonde and Takamoto.
responses.response: I understand his sense that topology is deeper physics, and I rank B058 among the strongest alternatives. My difficulty is the attribution. Kane, Mele and Molenkamp leave out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang for the HgTe prediction and Fu, Moore and Balents for three dimensions, and the 2016 topology prize sits close. I cannot answer that within three names, and I am not the person to judge the theory. I would therefore put B058 behind B030 for this year, and keep it on my alternatives list. On Lemonde and Takamoto, I think a short expert review is the proper way to settle it and it should be done before the vote.

responses.point: Danielsson still ranks B055 first but calls it the least supported candidate, concedes that attribution between WMAP and Planck is a genuine problem, and says he would not be unhappy to see B030 win.
responses.response: I value his candour. His trio of Bennett, Spergel and Puget and my trio of Bennett, Spergel and Page cannot both be defended, and I have not found a rule that makes either one fair. Page and Bennett built WMAP, Puget leads Planck/HFI, and any three exclude a team that did decisive work. Given his own statement that support is thin, I have dropped B055 from my alternatives. I would welcome the cosmology case being brought back with a clearly stated rule for WMAP and Planck, since the science is mature.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B030 first, says she may be biased upward because she is close to the lattice-clock field, and asks whether the theoretical magic-wavelength idea and the experimental realisation can be separated in the credit.
responses.response: Her disclosure is helpful and I think the committee should note it, but I would still follow her on the atomic physics. The theoretical idea and the first demonstration were Katori's, and Ye's contribution was accuracy and the many-body regime, so a two-name credit without a split is the fairest one I can see. I would not describe an exact share in the citation.

uncertainties: Whether expert reviewers find a priority claim by Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Hinkley or others strong enough to change the two-name credit.
Whether the committee accepts a precision-measurement invention as prize-level so soon after the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
Whether IceCube credit can be narrowed to three people fairly, which decides if B020 can ever be more than an alternative.
I found no second distinct part that fits within the three-person limit alongside Katori and Ye, so I propose a single-part prize.
statement.conflict_note: Updated from round 1: no change. I have no tie to Katori or Ye, and no recusal issue for B030. For B020 I disclose field proximity as a member of the Fermi-LAT collaboration, which contributed follow-up to the 2017 TXS 0506+056 observations, and I know the neutrino-astronomy community, though I have no known personal or institutional tie to Halzen, Karle or Spiering. I note the disclosures of Kroll, Olsson and Lindroth on B030 and see no reason for recusal, though they should be recorded; I support discounting Johansson's B029 ranking as he proposes.
